title: Money Mule Scams
content:
A money mule is a person used to receive, transfer, or withdraw money obtained through crime. Recruitment may happen through fake jobs, romance scams, social media, or stolen identity details.
Warning signs You are offered easy money for moving funds through your account. An online romantic contact asks you to hold or transfer money. A job requires your account to receive and forward payments. Someone sends money “by mistake” and asks you to forward it elsewhere. Stay safe Do not allow online contacts or unknown employers to use your account. Verify payment requests through an independent channel. Never share passwords, PINs, one-time codes, or identity documents. Contact your bank immediately if suspicious funds enter your account, and do not move them.

title: DNS64 & NAT64
content:
DNS64 & NAT64 DNS64 synthesizes IPv6 AAAA records from IPv4 A records when a domain has only IPv4 content. This is done by generating an IPv6 address that embeds the IPv4 address in the second portion of the address, while the first portion is a special IPv6 prefix used for NAT64 translation.
This NAT64 prefix is typically used by NAT64 gateways to translate IPv6 clients to IPv4 services when the destination only supports IPv4.

title: Online Sales Scams
content:
Online sales scams target buyers and sellers on fake stores and marketplaces. A fake seller may take payment without sending goods; a fake buyer may send a false payment notice or claim to have overpaid.
Warning signs The price is far below comparable listings. A seller refuses reasonable questions or has a new, incomplete profile. A buyer asks you to upgrade an account or refund an overpayment. A website lacks business details, contact information, privacy terms, or secure payment options. Stay safe Use trusted platforms and keep communications within the platform. Confirm money is in your account; do not rely on screenshots or emailed receipts. Check business details and research unfamiliar sellers. Do not refund alleged overpayments until the original payment has cleared.

title: One-Time Password
content:
One-Time Password (OTP) Hashing algorithms are used to generate one-time passwords. These algorithms use two inputs: a seed and a moving factor.
The seed is a fixed value, or secret key. This secret key is generated when a new account is enrolled with the authentication server. Based on the moving factor, there are two types of one-time passwords: HOTP and TOTP.
HOTP HOTP stands for Hash-based Message Authentication Code One-Time Password.
The HOTP algorithm is event-based. It uses a counter as the moving factor to generate a one-time password. In this case, an event is an increment of the counter.
The previously generated one-time password remains valid until the next one-time password is generated.
TOTP (TOTP) stands for Time-Based One-Time Password.
The TOTP algorithm uses time instead of a counter as the moving factor.
The length of time for which each password remains valid is called the time step.

title: Passwordless Authentication
content:
Passwordless Authentication Passwordless authentication is a type of multifactor authentication. Instead of the weak password factor, it uses stronger authentication factors such as a fingerprint or a secret PIN. Passwordless authentication relies on the cryptographic key-pair principles used by digital certificates: a private key and a public key.
An individual who wants to create a secure account uses a tool, such as a mobile application or browser extension, to generate a key pair consisting of a private key and a public key. The private key is stored on the user’s device and is bound to a factor such as a fingerprint, PIN, or voice recognition. It can be accessed only after the user provides that factor.
The public key is provided to the website, application, browser, or other online service where the user wants to maintain an account.
Public Key Infrastructure Card (PKI Card) Public Key Infrastructure is a cryptographic and cybersecurity framework that protects communication between websites and users.
Fast Identity Online (FIDO) Fast Identity Online (FIDO) authentication is an initiative created by a group of organizations to reduce reliance on multiple usernames and passwords.
YubiKey A security key is a small hardware device that resembles a USB drive. On supported platforms, it can be used as an additional authentication factor alongside your password.

title: Risk-Based Authentication
content:
Risk-Based Authentication / Adaptive Authentication Risk-based or adaptive authentication analyzes signals from multiple sources and calculates a risk score for a specific session.
Organizational policies define the action to be taken based on the calculated risk score.

title: Phishing
content:
Phishing uses email, text messages, social media, or phone calls to impersonate a trusted source and steal information or money. Text phishing is called smishing, and phone phishing is called vishing.
Warning signs A link or attachment in an unexpected message. Urgency, threats, or a claim that you will lose money or face penalties. Generic greetings, misspelled domains, unusual characters, or requests for credentials. A prize or competition requiring personal or financial details. Stay safe Do not use links supplied in unexpected messages; visit the organisation’s site directly. Never share passwords, card details, PINs, or one-time codes in response to a message or call. Enable multi-factor authentication and keep software updated. Avoid sensitive logins on public Wi-Fi and log out of important sessions when finished.

title: Phone Porting and SIM Swap Scams
content:
A phone porting or SIM swap scam transfers your mobile number to a SIM or eSIM controlled by a criminal. The criminal can receive calls, text messages, and SMS security codes used to access accounts.
Warning signs Your phone unexpectedly displays SOS or No service without an outage. You receive an unexpected notification about a new SIM or provider. You see unfamiliar logins or transactions and cannot receive security codes. Stay safe Set a security PIN with your telecommunications provider. Use authenticator apps or passkeys instead of SMS authentication where possible. Protect personal details, use unique passwords, and shred documents containing identity information. Contact your provider immediately if service stops unexpectedly, then contact your bank about suspicious activity.

title: Security Assertion Markup Language
content:
Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is a single sign-on protocol built on XML. It supports both authentication and authorization over SOAP/HTTP requests between an identity provider (IdP) and a service provider (SP).
Before communicating for identity verification, the two providers must define a SAML agreement and exchange initial information through metadata. This information includes details such as:
Public keys used for encryption, supported encryption protocols, and endpoint URLs that specify where SAML messages should be sent. Supported binding methods and supported XML attribute formats. Once both providers know these details about each other, they configure themselves accordingly.

title: Single Sign-On / Federation
content:
Single Sign-On / Federation (SSO/Federation) Federation (Different Domains) Federation is a trust relationship between two systems or organizations.
It defines where user credentials are stored and how those credentials can be used for authentication without exposing them to a third party.
Single Sign-On (Multiple Applications in One Domain) Single sign-on allows users to authenticate and access different applications in the same domain by signing in once through the identity provider and establishing a session.
It can also be used to provide single logout.

title: Quishing and QR Code Scams
content:
Quishing is phishing delivered through a QR code. A fraudulent code may open a fake login page, trigger an unsafe download, or send you to a payment site controlled by a criminal.
Warning signs The code arrives unexpectedly or is paired with urgency or threats. It is pasted over a legitimate code in a public place. The destination address looks unusual or asks for sensitive details. Stay safe Preview and inspect the web address after scanning before continuing. Type addresses manually for sensitive logins and payments. Download apps from official app stores rather than QR links. Keep devices updated, use multi-factor authentication, and avoid scanning unknown codes.

title: What is a Non-Fungible Token (NFT)?
content:
What is a Non-Fungible Token (NFT)? Non-fungible tokens or NFTs are cryptographic digital assets stored on a blockchain with unique identification codes and metadata that distinguish them from each other.
Unlike cryptocurrencies, NFTs cannot be traded or exchanged at equivalency because each token is unique and represents a distinct asset or right.
NFT Use Cases Digital artwork Real estate and property rights University degrees and identity credentials In-game items and avatars Domain names Event tickets Collectibles Important Note NFTs provide a public certificate of authenticity and proof of ownership, but they do not prevent copying or sharing the underlying digital file itself.

title: OpenID Connect
content:
OpenID Connect (OIDC) OIDC is a single sign-on protocol built on top of the OAuth 2.0 framework. It uses JSON-based Web Tokens (JWTs) to securely represent identity and authorization data.
A JWT is a standard used to define and securely exchange claims between the identity provider (IdP) and the relying party (RP). Claims can contain user attributes and other information needed to support identity verification.
OIDC scopes define the claims, or user attributes, that an application can access. The identity provider maintains a list of supported scopes and makes them available to the relying party, or application, after the user explicitly consents to share the requested information.
Before communication begins, the relying party and identity provider exchange metadata. Both parties must agree on the supported scopes. The identity provider provides the relying party with a client secret and client identifier. The relying party also shares endpoint URLs so that it can receive authorization codes and tokens.

title: Ransomware
content:
Ransomware is malicious software that encrypts files or blocks access to a device and demands payment. Criminals may also steal data and threaten to publish it.
How it spreads Suspicious links or attachments. Malicious websites or untrusted applications. Infected USB devices. Compromised accounts or online sessions. Signs and protection Locked files, unfamiliar extensions, disabled security tools, or a ransom note are warning signs. Keep software updated, use security protection, enable multi-factor authentication, restrict permissions, and back up important data. If attacked, record the details, disconnect the device and other devices from the network, and change important passwords from a clean device. Do not assume payment guarantees recovery.

title: Secure Web Gateway
content:
Secure Web Gateway (SWG) A secure web gateway is a security solution that prevents unsecured internet traffic from entering an organization’s internal network.
It helps protect users from malicious websites and supports regulatory compliance.
Core Functionality URL filtering Malicious code detection and filtering Application control for popular SaaS services Blocking access to malicious websites and links Enforcing web use policies Filtering traffic at the application level Difference from Firewalls and Proxies Firewalls inspect network-layer packets and compare them against known signatures. Proxies filter outbound or inbound connections based on policy. SWGs operate at the application layer and can evaluate web traffic more granularly. Architecture Summary SWGs sit between users and the internet, protecting good traffic while blocking malicious content and enforcing organizational policy.

title: Single Sign-On Protocol Comparison
content: Single Sign-On Protocol Comparison (SSO Protocol Comparison) A long-established authentication, authorization, and single sign-on protocol. Uses XML to exchange information. SAML assertions or tokens are relatively large and more difficult to process. Does not natively support user consent, although this can be achieved through additional development. Because it has been available for a long time, it is still trusted by many organizations, including government institutions. Well suited for enterprises and business-to-business information exchange. A newer single sign-on protocol built on the OAuth 2.0 framework. Uses JSON-based Web Tokens (JWTs), which are smaller and easier to process. Natively supports user consent. OIDC is increasingly providing features supported by SAML. Well suited for business-to-consumer information exchange. It also supports authentication for modern applications such as single-page applications (SPAs) and mobile applications.

title: Remote Access Scams
content:
A remote access scam tricks you into installing software or granting control of your computer or phone. The criminal may steal information, install malware, or access online banking.
Warning signs An unexpected caller or pop-up claims your device has a virus. Pressure to act immediately or pay with gift cards or unusual methods. A request to install remote-control software or log in to your bank. The cursor, settings, files, or performance change unexpectedly. Stay safe Never grant access to an unknown person who contacts you unexpectedly. Initiate support yourself through a verified official channel. Keep operating systems, security software, and applications updated. If access was granted, disconnect from the internet, scan the device, change sensitive passwords from another device, and contact your bank.

title: Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB)
content:
Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB) According to Gartner, a cloud access security broker is a security policy enforcement point placed between cloud service consumers and cloud service providers.
CASBs aggregate enterprise security policies and enforce them as cloud resources are accessed.
Common CASB Features Authentication and single sign-on Authorization and credential mapping Device profiling Encryption and tokenization Logging and alerting Malware detection and prevention Data loss prevention and activity monitoring Shadow IT detection Scope CASBs are mainly used to protect SaaS applications in the cloud. Their support for PaaS and IaaS is usually more limited.
Deployment Modes Proxy mode API mode Use Cases Shadow IT discovery and governance Data exfiltration prevention Threat detection and forensic investigation Compliance support and activity monitoring

title: Scam Calls and Spam Calls
content:
A scam call uses a phone conversation to impersonate a trusted organisation or person and obtain information or money. Spam calls are unwanted marketing, but scam calls may include deception, threats, or requests for payment.
Warning signs An unknown, overseas, hidden, or unexpected number. Requests for passwords, banking details, payments, or remote access. Threats of arrest, fines, service disconnection, or other consequences. An offer of guaranteed investment returns or an unusually cheap service. Stay safe Let unknown calls go to voicemail and hang up when a request seems suspicious. Call the organisation back using a trusted number, not one supplied by the caller. Enable phone spam filtering and block or report suspicious numbers. Keep personal contact details private and never share PINs or passwords by phone.

title: Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA)
content:
Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) Zero trust network access, also known as the software-defined perimeter, is a set of technologies and functionalities that enable secure access to internal applications for remote users.
Core Principle Trust is never implicit. Access is granted on a need-to-know, least-privileged basis defined by granular policy.
Key Benefits Remote users get seamless and secure access to private applications Applications are not exposed directly to the internet Network access is separated from application access Risk from compromised devices is reduced Access is limited to specific applications, not full network reachability Lateral movement risk is reduced Deployment Model ZTNA uses user-to-application access patterns rather than traditional network-based trust assumptions. It often relies on end-to-end encrypted TLS micro-tunnels.

title: Scam Text Messages
content:
Scam text messages, also called smishing, use SMS to impersonate an organisation or family member. They commonly contain a link or phone number designed to steal information, install malware, or obtain payment.
Common scenarios A fake account alert or refund. An unpaid toll or parcel redirection request. A message from a supposed child using a new number. Stay safe Pause and do not click links or call numbers in unexpected texts. Verify the request using a known number or official app. Never send personal or banking information by text. Block and report the sender, enable spam filtering, and contact your bank immediately if details were shared.

title: Social Media Scams
content:
Social media scams use profiles, posts, messages, advertisements, and marketplaces to obtain money or personal information.
Common forms Fake profiles of friends, relatives, celebrities, charities, or businesses. Marketplace listings, fake prizes, and investment offers. Fake employment offers and malicious links on professional networks. Stay safe Keep profiles private and limit public personal details such as location, birth date, and phone number. Enable multi-factor authentication and use unique passwords. Verify unexpected contacts; reverse-search profile images when appropriate. Never send money, sensitive information, or intimate media to someone known only online.

title: Spoof Calls and Fake Caller IDs
content:
Caller ID spoofing falsifies the number or name displayed on your phone so a criminal appears to be a trusted person or organisation. The caller may then seek money or personal information.
Warning signs An unexpected call appears to come from a familiar organisation. The caller creates urgency, threatens consequences, or asks for sensitive details. The caller cannot provide a reference you can verify independently. Stay safe Do not trust caller ID as proof of identity. Let unexpected calls go to voicemail or hang up when anything feels wrong. Call back using an official number you already know. Enable built-in call filtering or a reputable screening service and report suspicious calls.

title: Unexpected Money and Inheritance Scams
content:
Unexpected-money scams claim that you have won a prize, inherited money, or are owed a payment. The criminal asks for personal details, an upfront fee, or access to an account before releasing the supposed funds.
Common scenarios Lottery or competition prize claims. An inheritance from an unknown relative. A tax refund or other unexpected payment. Warning signs and protection Unexpected contact, time pressure, requests for passwords, or a fee to claim money. Do not click links or share PINs, passwords, banking details, or one-time codes. Verify claims through an independently sourced official contact. Legitimate winnings or refunds do not require you to pay an upfront fee to receive them.
